When Elon Musk was just 12 years old, he taught himself computer programming and created a video game called Blastar.

He sold the full game (source code included) to a South African computer magazine for $500.
At 12.

Most kids that age were playing games.
Elon was already building and selling them.
This was the very first money he ever made from code — a small but clear sign of the relentless builder he would become.

Elon Musk has been obsessed with the letter 𝕏 for over 25 years.

Back in the late 90s, he named his first major company X.com — a bold attempt to create the “everything app” for finance.
After it became PayPal, he still couldn’t let go of the letter.

Fast forward to 2023: he bought Twitter and immediately rebranded it to 𝕏

Here’s a classic photo of young Elon proudly holding up the original black X.com debit card:
Photo of Elon holding the X card
From X.com in 1999 to X (the everything app) in 2023+, the letter X has always been central to Elon’s vision.

He didn’t just pick a cool letter.

He’s been building toward the same idea for a quarter century.

Legacy media is terminally blind.

KTLA opens with: ‘Would you want to be in a car that… can’t be driven?’

Then spends 44 seconds clutching pearls over Tesla’s Cybercab — a purpose-built robotaxi with no steering wheel, no pedals, no side mirrors — because if it ‘runs into trouble,’ apparently only a tow truck can help.

Bro, that’s the entire point.

This isn’t a ‘problem.’ It’s the future: fully autonomous ride-hailing designed from the ground up to compete with Uber and Lyft, without the dead weight of human controls. 

Tesla is already gearing up for production, while this guy acts like removing a steering wheel is some shocking, dangerous experiment instead of the logical endpoint of self-driving tech that’s already operating on roads today (hello, Waymo in LA).

Legacy outlets can’t see the revolution even when it’s gliding past them on camera. No wonder trust in media is in the toilet.
Cybercab isn’t ‘undrivable.’ 

It’s driverless by design — and that’s exactly why it’s brilliant.”

SpaceX has confidentially submitted its S-1 registration statement in early April 2026, aiming for a massive $1.75 trillion valuation and a potential raise of up to $75 billion. If it goes through as planned, this could become the biggest IPO in history, with shares possibly starting to trade publicly in June or July.
The filing shows Starlink delivering a solid $4.42 billion in operating income for 2025, which helps counterbalance the $6.4 billion operating loss at xAI. Meanwhile, the company’s capital expenditures have surged dramatically—reaching $20.74 billion last year, about five times higher than just two years earlier—as it ramps up spending on rockets, satellites, and ground infrastructure.
Elon Musk’s base salary remains modest at $54,080 for 2025, and the structure includes dual-class shares that will let him maintain voting control even after the company goes public. This setup is fairly standard for fast-growing tech firms that want to protect long-term strategy from short-term market pressures.
